paras: The lynching of Allen Sturgis took place at Thomson, McDuffie County, Georgia, on the night of June 2-3, 1888, when men broke into the town jail, took Sturgis, a young Black man held on burglary charges, and hanged him from an oak beside a road at the edge of town. A coroner's jury found that he died "by parties to us unknown." Local reports called it the first lynching ever in McDuffie County, and brief wire and digest items carried it across the country.

In the spring of 1888 Thomson residents complained of burglaries and attempted entries into houses, often, according to local reports, into rooms occupied by women. According to the McDuffie Journal, as quoted by the Atlanta Constitution, Mrs. Willie Burnside of Augusta, visiting her mother Mrs. Basford, woke about 1 a.m. on Monday, May 28, to find a man under her bed. Neighbors pulled out Allen Sturgis, "colored, about 20 years old," who an Augusta dispatch said was whipped and then confessed to belonging to a burglary gang.

Warrants were issued for four alleged accomplices, who were bailed after a commitment trial, while Sturgis was bound over to the fall term of the superior court. The Augusta dispatch reported that "Threats of lynching were freely indulged in" on the town's streets.

During the night of Saturday, June 2, men broke open the jail door with a sledge hammer and took Sturgis about half a mile, just outside the town limits. With his arms and legs tied, he was hanged from a large oak about 15 feet from the road from Wrightsboro, and his neck was broken. The Constitution's correspondent wrote that it was done so quietly "that even the night marshal was not aware of it." The body was left hanging until the coroner arrived about 11 o'clock on Sunday morning, and large crowds went to see it.

Coroner James P. Johnson's jury returned its verdict that morning. Both Georgia reports said his mother refused the body, which was to be turned over to the medical college at Augusta, and asserted that "Even the colored people approve of the step taken," a claim from white correspondents only. No report of an arrest of the lynchers or of grand jury action appears in the coverage.

The fullest accounts came from Georgia: a Thomson dispatch in the Savannah Morning News on June 4 and a Thomson special in the Atlanta Constitution on June 5 headed "STURGIS STRETCHED," which shared much of its wording. The Savannah paper called Sturgis "an unmitigated rascal," and the Constitution said the lynchers "acted with discretion" and that the body would be "a good warning to both white and black."

Outside Georgia, an Atlanta wire printed June 4 in Wheeling, San Antonio and Indianapolis called him "the miscreant," and the Washington Evening Star named him "Alice sturgis." An Augusta special in the True Northerner of Michigan, headed "A Negro Ruffian Found Under a Woman's Bed Is Lynched," tied him to "an organized band of incendiaries and robbers." Weekly digests in the River Falls Journal, Kenosha Telegraph, Western Appeal, Chicago Citizen, Huntsville Gazette and Grenada Sentinel reduced the story to one sentence about a prisoner jailed "for robbery and incendiarism" and lynched by "a gang of masked men," often under the name "Hurgis." The New York Evening World said he was lynched "for assaulting a white woman."

The Thomson accounts put his capture on Monday, May 28, while the Atlanta wire said Friday night. The charge ranged from burglary and entering women's rooms in local reports to robbery and incendiarism in the digests and assault in the Evening World. The Augusta special placed the hanging "in the public street," but two Thomson reports put it beside the road outside town.

reader.title: Lynching of Allen Sturgis
bases: Men broke into the Thomson jail, took Allen Sturgis from his cell and hanged him from an oak by the road, and the inquest found death 'by parties to us unknown' (A2, A8, A11).

Sturgis, held for trial on burglary charges, was taken from jail and hanged by men the papers call a 'band', a 'mob' and 'a gang of masked men', with no lawful authority (A2, A3, A8, A12); the local reports frame it as punishment for his alleged crimes and lynch law taken when patience ran out (A2, A8).

A Thomson dispatch (A2), a Thomson special quoting the McDuffie Journal (A8), an Augusta wire (A11) and an Atlanta wire (A3) agree that Sturgis was taken from the Thomson jail and hanged on the night of June 2-3.

accounts.label: Thomson correspondents / McDuffie Journal
accounts.gist: A quiet, deliberate band broke the jail and hanged Sturgis on the town's outskirts; residents, and allegedly Black residents too, approved of punishing a burglar who had entered women's rooms.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Sturgis died by hanging on Saturday night, June 2, 1888, 'by parties to us unknown'.

accounts.label: Atlanta wire
accounts.gist: Sturgis was pulled from under a lady's bed on Friday night and jailed; the next night a mob broke into the jail and hanged him to a tree.

accounts.label: Augusta wires
accounts.gist: One version follows the Thomson details closely (A11); an Augusta special ties Sturgis to an organized band of incendiaries and robbers and puts the hanging in the public street (A9).

accounts.label: Weekly digest
accounts.gist: Sturgis, jailed for robbery and incendiarism, was taken out on the 3d by a gang of masked men and lynched.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News called Sturgis 'an unmitigated rascal' and said everybody agreed it was 'no more than what he deserved'.
The Atlanta Constitution's 'STURGIS STRETCHED' said the lynchers 'acted with discretion' and the body would be 'a good warning to both white and black'.
Atlanta and Augusta wires called him 'the miscreant' and 'A Negro Ruffian' without comment on the lynchers.
Weekly digests gave a one-sentence item, often with the name garbled to 'Hurgis' or 'Hurois'.
